q: What is planned value (PV)?
options: The money actually spent so far
The authorized budget assigned to the work scheduled to be done by a point in time
The budget of the work actually completed
The expected total cost of the project
explanation: Planned value is the authorized budget assigned to scheduled work. It shows how much work should have been accomplished by the data date.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Earned value (EV) analysis

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Earned value (EV) analysis

q: What is earned value (EV)?
options: The profit the project has earned
The realized cost of the work performed
The measure of work performed, expressed in terms of the budget authorized for that work
explanation: Earned value is the budget associated with the authorized work that has been completed. It ignores what the work actually cost.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Earned value (EV) analysis

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Earned value (EV) analysis

q: A project has a budget at completion of $200,000 and is 40% complete. What is the earned value?
explanation: EV = percent complete × BAC = 0.40 × $200,000 = $80,000.

q: EV is $80,000 and AC is $100,000. What is the cost variance, and what does it mean?
explanation: CV = EV − AC = 80,000 − 100,000 = −$20,000. A negative cost variance means the project is over the planned cost.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide Table 5-1; The Standard for Earned Value Management, 4.4.1.1

links.label: The Standard for Earned Value Management, 4.4.1.1

q: EV is $80,000 and PV is $70,000. What is the schedule variance, and what does it mean?
explanation: SV = EV − PV = 80,000 − 70,000 = +$10,000. A positive schedule variance means more work has been done than planned.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide Table 5-1; The Standard for Earned Value Management, 4.4.1.2

links.label: The Standard for Earned Value Management, 4.4.1.2

q: EV is $50,000 and AC is $40,000. What is the cost performance index?
explanation: CPI = EV ÷ AC = 50,000 ÷ 40,000 = 1.25. Above 1.0 means the project is under the planned cost.

q: EV is $45,000 and PV is $60,000. What is the schedule performance index?
explanation: SPI = EV ÷ PV = 45,000 ÷ 60,000 = 0.75. Below 1.0 means the project is behind schedule.

q: A project has a CPI of 0.8. What does this mean?
options: The project is 20% ahead of schedule
The project will finish 20% under budget
For every $1 spent, the project gets 80 cents of work
explanation: A CPI of 0.8 means that for every unit of cost incurred, only 0.8 of work was accomplished. The project is over budget.
ref: The Standard for Earned Value Management, 4.4.1.3

links.label: The Standard for Earned Value Management, 4.4.1.3

q: A project reports a CPI of 1.1 and an SPI of 0.9. What is its status?
options: Over budget and ahead of schedule
Under budget and ahead of schedule
explanation: CPI above 1.0 means under budget. SPI below 1.0 means behind schedule. Cost and schedule are judged separately.

q: BAC is $500,000 and the CPI is 0.8. Current cost performance is expected to continue. What is the estimate at completion?
explanation: When the CPI is expected to stay the same, EAC = BAC ÷ CPI = 500,000 ÷ 0.8 = $625,000.

q: EAC is $625,000 and AC is $250,000. What is the estimate to complete?
explanation: ETC = EAC − AC = 625,000 − 250,000 = $375,000. This is the expected cost of the remaining work.

q: BAC is $500,000 and EAC is $625,000. What is the variance at completion?
options: +$125,000, expected to finish ahead of schedule
explanation: VAC = BAC − EAC = 500,000 − 625,000 = −$125,000. A negative value is a projected budget deficit.

q: BAC is $100,000, EV is $40,000 and AC is $50,000. The overrun was caused by a one-time event, and the remaining work is expected to go as planned. What is the EAC?
explanation: If future work will be done at the planned rate, EAC = AC + (BAC − EV) = 50,000 + 60,000 = $110,000.

q: BAC is $100,000, EV is $40,000 and AC is $50,000. What TCPI is needed to finish within the original budget?
explanation: TCPI = (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC) = 60,000 ÷ 50,000 = 1.20. Each remaining dollar must produce $1.20 of work.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, To-complete performance index (TCPI)

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, To-complete performance index (TCPI)

q: A TCPI greater than 1.0 means:
options: The remaining work must be done more efficiently than planned, so the goal is harder to meet
The project is ahead of schedule
The project can relax its cost control
explanation: TCPI is work remaining divided by funds remaining. Above 1.0 there is more work left than money, so the target is harder to achieve.

q: A $40,000 project is planned evenly over 4 weeks. At the end of week 2, the work is 40% complete and $22,000 has been spent. What is the schedule variance?
In the same project (BAC $40,000, 40% complete at the end of week 2, $22,000 spent), what is the CPI?
explanation: EV = $16,000 and AC = $22,000. CPI = EV ÷ AC = 16,000 ÷ 22,000 = 0.73. The project is over budget.

q: A $5,000 work package is 80% finished. The project uses the 0/100 rule. How much earned value is credited?
explanation: The 0/100 method gives no credit for partial work. The full $5,000 is earned only when the work package is complete.
ref: The Standard for Earned Value Management, 3.2.2.2

links.label: The Standard for Earned Value Management, 3.2.2.2

q: An $8,000 work package has started but is not finished. The project uses the 50/50 rule. How much earned value is credited?
explanation: With the 50/50 rule, 50% is credited when the work starts and the remaining 50% when it is completed: 0.5 × $8,000 = $4,000.
ref: The Standard for Earned Value Management, 3.2.2.2

links.label: The Standard for Earned Value Management, 3.2.2.2

q: Which three baselines are integrated to form the performance measurement baseline?
explanation: Earned value management integrates the scope baseline with the cost baseline and schedule baseline to form the performance measurement baseline.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Earned value (EV) analysis

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Earned value (EV) analysis

q: Does planned value include management reserve?
options: Only at the end of the project
explanation: Planned value is the authorized budget planned for the work, not including management reserve.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Earned value (EV) analysis

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Earned value (EV) analysis

q: Which earned value method is used for work that cannot be measured, such as project management support?
explanation: Level of effort is used for nonmeasurable work and earns value with the passage of time. It should be kept to a minimum because it cannot show a schedule variance.
ref: The Standard for Earned Value Management, 3.2.2.2

links.label: The Standard for Earned Value Management, 3.2.2.2

q: Which statement is true of all the variance and index formulas (CV, SV, CPI, SPI)?
options: Earned value comes first in each formula
Actual cost comes first in each formula
Planned value comes first in each formula
They all use the budget at completion
explanation: CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV, CPI = EV ÷ AC, SPI = EV ÷ PV. Earned value is always first; cost formulas use AC and schedule formulas use PV.

q: Which question does the estimate at completion (EAC) answer?
options: How much has been spent so far?
How much work should be done by now?
How much more will it cost from now?
What is the whole project now expected to cost?
explanation: EAC is the expected total cost of completing all the work: actual cost to date plus the estimate to complete.
